For an antipodal set X, the sum of harmonic polynomials of degree 2k is related to the 2k-th moment tensor. If all odd moments vanish (by antipodality), the condition for degree 2 to be in Hst(X) is that the inertia tensor is proportional to the identity. If degree 2 is not in Hst(X), the inertia tensor has distinct eigenvalues. Use representation theory of O(d+1) to show that if a higher even moment vanishes, then the inertia tensor must be isotropic, forcing degree 2 to vanish. Alternatively, construct a counterexample by finding an antipodal set with Hst(X) containing 4 but not 2.

concept.title: Escher Staircases in Algebra: Infinite Ascending Chains That Loop Back
concept.concept_description: An Escher staircase is an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals I_1 strictly contained in I_2 strictly contained in ... that nevertheless has I_1 as an element of the infinite intersection. This seems impossible — how can an infinite ascending chain loop back to the beginning? But in the ring of integer-valued polynomials Int(Z), the chain I_n = {f in Int(Z) : f(Z) contained in 2^n Z} is strictly ascending (I_n strictly contained in I_{n+1}) yet the intersection of all I_n is {0}, which contains the zero polynomial that is also in I_1. Conjecture: Every non-Noetherian ring contains an Escher staircase, and the 'height' of the Escher effect (measured by the Krull dimension gap) is a new ring invariant. For Int(Z), the Escher height is infinite (the chain never stabilizes). For Z[x_1, x_2, ...], the Escher height equals the number of variables. For the p-adic integers Z_p, there is NO Escher staircase (Z_p is a DVR, hence Noetherian). Test: prove that Int(Z) has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Prove that k[x_1,...,x_n] has Escher height n. Compute the Escher height for the ring of all algebraic integers. Impact: a new invariant for non-Noetherian rings that measures how far a ring is from being Noetherian — the algebraic equivalent of Escher's impossible architecture.

open MvPolynomial

namespace EscherStaircase

/-- An **Escher staircase** in a commutative ring `R`: an infinite strictly
ascending chain of ideals `I 0 ⊊ I 1 ⊊ ⋯`. -/
def HasEscherStaircase (R : Type*) [CommRing R] : Prop :=
  ∃ I : ℕ → Ideal R, StrictMono I

/-- The "loop back" of the Escher staircase is content-free: `0` lies in the
bottom step `I 0` and in every step, hence in the whole intersection. -/
theorem escher_loops_back {R : Type*} [CommRing R] (I : ℕ → Ideal R) :
    (0 : R) ∈ I 0 ∧ ∀ n, (0 : R) ∈ I n := by
  exact ⟨zero_mem _, fun n => zero_mem _⟩

/-- Order-theoretic core: if the strict order on `α` is not well-founded (there
is no descending sequence), then there is a strictly increasing sequence
`ℕ → α`.  Extracted from a non-stabilising monotone chain. -/
theorem exists_strictMono_of_not_wellFoundedGT {α : Type*} [PartialOrder α]
    (h : ¬ WellFoundedGT α) : ∃ f : ℕ → α, StrictMono f := by
  rw [wellFoundedGT_iff_monotone_chain_condition] at h
  push_neg at h
  obtain ⟨a, ha⟩ := h
  set idx : ℕ → ℕ := fun k => Nat.rec 0 (fun _ prev => (ha prev).choose) k with hidx
  have hstep : ∀ k, a (idx k) < a (idx (k + 1)) := by
    intro k
    have hspec := (ha (idx k)).choose_spec
    exact lt_of_le_of_ne (a.monotone hspec.1) hspec.2
  exact ⟨fun k => a (idx k), strictMono_nat_of_lt_succ hstep⟩

/-- **Escher ⟺ non-Noetherian.**  A commutative ring admits an Escher staircase
(an infinite strictly ascending chain of ideals) if and only if it is not a
Noetherian ring. -/
theorem hasEscherStaircase_iff_not_isNoetherianRing (R : Type*) [CommRing R] :
    HasEscherStaircase R ↔ ¬ IsNoetherianRing R := by
  rw [isNoetherianRing_iff, isNoetherian_iff']
  constructor
  · rintro ⟨I, hI⟩ hwf
    exact not_strictMono_of_wellFoundedGT I hI
  · intro h
    exact exists_strictMono_of_not_wellFoundedGT h

/-- A Noetherian ring has no Escher staircase. -/
theorem not_hasEscherStaircase_of_isNoetherianRing (R : Type*) [CommRing R]
    [IsNoetherianRing R] : ¬ HasEscherStaircase R := by
  rw [hasEscherStaircase_iff_not_isNoetherianRing]
  exact fun h => h ‹_›

/-!
### The infinite-height example: `k[x₀, x₁, x₂, …]`
-/

/-- The `n`-th step of the canonical staircase in `k[x₀,x₁,…]`: the ideal
generated by the first `n` variables `x₀, …, x_{n-1}`. -/
noncomputable def varChain (k : Type*) [Field k] (n : ℕ) :
    Ideal (MvPolynomial ℕ k) :=
  Ideal.span (MvPolynomial.X '' {i | i < n})

/-- The `n`-th variable `xₙ` is not in the ideal generated by the earlier
variables `x₀, …, x_{n-1}`. -/
theorem X_not_mem_varChain (k : Type*) [Field k] (n : ℕ) :
    (MvPolynomial.X n : MvPolynomial ℕ k) ∉ varChain k n := by
  intro hmem
  set f : ℕ → MvPolynomial ℕ k := fun i => if i < n then 0 else X i with hf
  set φ : MvPolynomial ℕ k →ₐ[k] MvPolynomial ℕ k := aeval f with hφ
  have hker : varChain k n ≤ RingHom.ker (φ : MvPolynomial ℕ k →+* MvPolynomial ℕ k) := by
    rw [varChain, Ideal.span_le]
    rintro y ⟨i, hi, rfl⟩
    simp only [Set.mem_setOf_eq] at hi
    rw [SetLike.mem_coe, RingHom.mem_ker]
    show φ (X i) = 0
    rw [hφ, aeval_X]
    simp [hf, hi]
  have hzero : φ (X n) = 0 := by
    have := hker hmem
    rwa [RingHom.mem_ker] at this
  rw [aeval_X] at hzero
  simp only [hf, lt_irrefl, if_false] at hzero
  exact X_ne_zero n hzero

/-- The variable chain is strictly increasing. -/
theorem varChain_strictMono (k : Type*) [Field k] :
    StrictMono (varChain k) := by
  apply strictMono_nat_of_lt_succ
  intro n
  rw [lt_iff_le_and_ne]
  refine ⟨?_, ?_⟩
  · apply Ideal.span_mono
    apply Set.image_mono
    intro i hi
    exact lt_trans hi (Nat.lt_succ_self n)
  · intro hEq
    apply X_not_mem_varChain k n
    rw [hEq]
    apply Ideal.subset_span
    exact ⟨n, Nat.lt_succ_self n, rfl⟩

/-- **The polynomial ring in countably many variables has an Escher staircase.**
This is the "infinite height" case: the chain `(x₀) ⊊ (x₀,x₁) ⊊ ⋯` never
stabilises. -/
theorem hasEscherStaircase_mvPolynomial_nat (k : Type*) [Field k] :
    HasEscherStaircase (MvPolynomial ℕ k) :=
  ⟨varChain k, varChain_strictMono k⟩

/-!
### Noetherian rings: no staircase
-/

/-- The integers — a PID, the algebraic analogue of the `p`-adic integers `ℤ_p`
(a DVR) — have no Escher staircase. -/
theorem not_hasEscherStaircase_int : ¬ HasEscherStaircase ℤ :=
  not_hasEscherStaircase_of_isNoetherianRing ℤ

/-- The polynomial ring in *finitely* many variables `k[x₀,…,x_{n-1}]` is
Noetherian (Hilbert basis theorem), hence has no Escher staircase.  Contrast
with `hasEscherStaircase_mvPolynomial_nat`. -/
theorem not_hasEscherStaircase_mvPolynomial_fin (k : Type*) [Field k] (n : ℕ) :
    ¬ HasEscherStaircase (MvPolynomial (Fin n) k) :=
  not_hasEscherStaircase_of_isNoetherianRing (MvPolynomial (Fin n) k)

end EscherStaircase

# Computational Evidence — Escher Staircases

## 1. Small-case calculations in `k[x₀, x₁, x₂, …]`

Let `Jₙ = (x₀, …, x_{n-1})` be the ideal generated by the first `n` variables
(`J₀ = (0)` is the zero ideal). The claim is `Jₙ ⊊ J_{n+1}` for every `n`.

| n | Jₙ generators | New variable `xₙ` | In `Jₙ`? | In `J_{n+1}`? |
|---|---------------|-------------------|----------|----------------|
| 0 | ∅ (zero ideal)| x₀                | no       | yes            |
| 1 | x₀            | x₁                | no       | yes            |
| 2 | x₀, x₁        | x₂                | no       | yes            |
| 3 | x₀, x₁, x₂    | x₃                | no       | yes            |

**Separating witness.** For each `n`, the algebra endomorphism
`φₙ : k[x₀,x₁,…] → k[x₀,x₁,…]` defined by `φₙ(xᵢ) = 0` if `i < n` and
`φₙ(xᵢ) = xᵢ` otherwise kills every generator of `Jₙ` but sends `xₙ ↦ xₙ ≠ 0`.
Hence `xₙ ∉ Jₙ` while `xₙ ∈ J_{n+1}`, so the inclusion is strict. This is exactly
the argument formalised in `X_not_mem_varChain`.

The "loop back": `0 ∈ J₀` and `0 ∈ Jₙ` for all `n`, so `0` lies in the whole
intersection ⋂ Jₙ. This holds because `0` is a member of every ideal, which is
why the loop-back phenomenon is content-free (`escher_loops_back`).

## 2. Noetherian counter-tests (no staircase expected)

| Ring | Noetherian? | Escher staircase? |
|------|-------------|-------------------|
| `ℤ` (PID) | yes | no |
| `ℤ_p` (DVR) | yes | no |
| `k[x₀,…,x_{n-1}]` (finite vars) | yes (Hilbert basis) | no |
| `k[x₀,x₁,x₂,…]` (countable vars) | no | yes (explicit chain above) |
| ring of all algebraic integers | no | yes (see below) |

Every column is consistent with the equivalence
`HasEscherStaircase R ↔ ¬ IsNoetherianRing R`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

The conjecture "every non-Noetherian ring has an Escher staircase" is *not* a
counterexample target — it is provably equivalent to the definition of failing
the ascending chain condition (`hasEscherStaircase_iff_not_isNoetherianRing`).
No counterexample can exist for commutative rings.

The tempting over-claim "the loop-back is a special feature of `Int(ℤ)`" is
**false**: `0` belongs to every ideal in every ring, so the loop-back is
universal and carries no information. This falsification reshaped the project
toward the strict-ascension content.

## 4. The ring of all algebraic integers

Chain: `(2^{1/2}) ⊊ (2^{1/4}) ⊊ (2^{1/8}) ⊊ ⋯`. Each `2^{1/2^{k+1}}` divides
`2^{1/2^k}` but not conversely (valuation halves each step), so the chain is
strictly ascending. Hence the ring of all algebraic integers is non-Noetherian
and has an Escher staircase of infinite height. Formalising the requisite
valuation theory is deferred (see future directions).

# Future Directions — Escher Staircases in Algebra

## 1. A quantitative Escher height via Krull dimension

Move beyond the Boolean "staircase exists or not" to a genuine numerical
invariant. Define the Escher height of a ring as the supremum, over all strictly
ascending chains of prime ideals participating in an infinite ascending chain, of
the Krull-dimension gap between the top and bottom of the loop. For a polynomial
ring in `n` variables over a field one expects this height to equal `n`, and for
the ring of integer-valued polynomials to be infinite.

The key insight is that the *existence* of a strictly ascending chain is
equivalent to non-Noetherianness and therefore carries no fine structure, so any
non-trivial invariant must be extracted from the prime spectrum rather than from
the chain of ideals itself. Why now? The equivalence between ascending chains and
failure of the ascending chain condition is now settled, which isolates exactly
the place — Krull dimension of the associated primes — where new information must
live.

## 2. Escher staircases in the ring of all algebraic integers

Show that the ring of all algebraic integers admits an explicit infinite strictly
ascending chain of principal ideals, for instance the chain generated by the
successive dyadic roots of two, whose valuations halve at each step. Conclude the
ring is non-Noetherian and compute its Escher height as infinite.

The key insight is that although the ring of all algebraic integers is a Bezout
domain in which every finitely generated ideal is principal, its value group is
divisible, so principal ideals can shrink forever without ever terminating. Why
now? Valuation-theoretic tools for infinite algebraic extensions are mature enough
to make the halving-valuation chain fully rigorous, turning a folklore example
into a precise theorem.

## 3. The dual staircase: descending chains that loop back

Investigate the mirror image of an Escher staircase: an infinite strictly
*descending* chain of ideals `I₀ ⊋ I₁ ⊋ ⋯` whose union is a proper ideal, the
Artinian-side impossible staircase. Characterise exactly which rings admit such a
descending staircase and relate it to the failure of the descending chain
condition.

The key insight is that ascending and descending chain conditions are genuinely
independent, so the descending staircase detects a different form of infinitude —
one visible in valuation rings of infinite rank rather than in polynomial rings.
Why now? With the ascending picture pinned to non-Noetherianness, the descending
analogue is the natural next coordinate for classifying how far a ring sits from
being both Noetherian and Artinian.

## 4. Integer-valued polynomials and the binomial staircase

Formalise the ring of integer-valued polynomials and its canonical filtration by
the ideals of polynomials whose values are divisible by increasing powers of a
fixed prime. Prove these form a strictly ascending chain, giving a second, purely
number-theoretic, infinite-height example distinct from the polynomial ring in
countably many variables.

The key insight is that the binomial coefficient polynomials form a module basis
that is not a ring-theoretic finite generating set, which is precisely what forces
the chain to ascend without stabilising. Why now? The module structure of
integer-valued polynomials over the binomial basis is well understood, so the only
remaining obstacle is packaging it as an explicit non-stabilising ideal chain.

chain condition provides a rigorous foundation on which additive behaviour under
ring operations can finally be tested and proved.

concept.concept_description: The Fibonacci sequence is defined by F(n+1) = F(n) + F(n-1) and converges to the golden ratio. Define the ANTI-Fibonacci sequence: A(n+1) is the smallest positive integer that is NOT equal to A(n) + A(n-1). The sequence begins 1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, ...   | 0 => 1

@[simp] theorem A_succ (k : ℕ) : A (k + 1) = A k + k := rfl

/-- Every term is positive (so consecutive ratios are well defined). -/

/-- **Main theorem 1 (closed form).** `2 · A k + k = k² + 2`, i.e.
`A k = 1 + k(k-1)/2`.  Proved by induction; the step is pure arithmetic on the
inductive hypothesis. -/

  induction' k with k ih <;> norm_num [ * ] at * ; linarith

/-- Real-valued closed form: `A k = (k² - k + 2)/2`. -/

    Tendsto (fun k => (A k : ℝ) / (k : ℝ) ^ 2) atTop (𝓝 (1 / 2)) := by
  -- We'll use the fact that $A(k) = \frac{k^2 - k + 2}{2}$ to rewrite the limit expression.
  suffices h_suff : Filter.Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => ((k^2 - k + 2) / 2 : ℝ) / k^2) Filter.atTop (nhds (1 / 2)) by
    convert h_suff using 2 ; rw [ A_real_closed ];
  -- Simplify the expression inside the limit.
  suffices h_simp : Filter.Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => (1 - 1 / (k : ℝ) + 2 / (k ^ 2 : ℝ)) / 2) Filter.atTop (nhds (1 / 2)) by

    Tendsto (fun k : ℕ => (k : ℝ) / (A k : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 0) := by
  -- Using the closed form, we can express $k / A k$ as $2k / (k^2 - k + 2)$.
  have h_closed_form : ∀ k : ℕ, (k : ℝ) / (A k) = 2 * (k : ℝ) / ((k : ℝ) ^ 2 - (k : ℝ) + 2) := by

  rw [ Metric.tendsto_nhds ] ; norm_num;
  exact fun ε hε => ⟨ Nat.ceil ( 2 + ε⁻¹ * 4 ), fun n hn => by rw [ h_closed_form ] ; rw [ div_lt_iff₀ ] <;> nlinarith [ Nat.ceil_le.mp hn, inv_pos.2 hε, mul_inv_cancel₀ hε.ne' ] ⟩

/-- Auxiliary: the consecutive ratio tends to `1` (no golden ratio, no oscillation). -/
theorem A_ratio_tendsto_one :
    Tendsto (fun k => (A (k + 1) : ℝ) / (A k : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 1) := by
  convert Tendsto.const_add 1 ( A_lin_div_tendsto_zero ) using 2;
  · rw [ add_div' ] <;> norm_cast <;> norm_num [ A_succ ];
    exact ne_of_gt ( A_pos _ );
  · norm_num

ratio does **not** tend to the golden ratio `φ`, in contrast with the Fibonacci ratio
(`tendsto_fib_succ_div_fib_atTop`).  Since the anti-Fibonacci ratio tends to `1` and
`1 < φ`, uniqueness of limits forbids convergence to `φ`. -/
theorem antiFib_avoids_goldenRatio :
    ¬ Tendsto (fun k => (A (k + 1) : ℝ) / (A k : ℝ)) atTop (𝓝 φ) := by
  by_contra h_contra
  have h1 : (1 : ℝ) = φ := tendsto_nhds_unique A_ratio_tendsto_one h_contra
  linarith [Real.one_lt_goldenRatio]

to the golden ratio `φ` (Mathlib's `tendsto_fib_succ_div_fib_atTop`), whereas the
*anti-Fibonacci* consecutive ratio provably does **not**.  The two additive recurrences
`F (k+1) = F k + F (k-1)` and `A (k+1) = A k + k` thus have genuinely different

  ⟨tendsto_fib_succ_div_fib_atTop, antiFib_avoids_goldenRatio⟩

end AntiFibonacci

Direct evaluation (`#eval (List.range 12).map A`) gives

```

```

(`#eval (List.range 12).map (fun k => 1 + k*(k-1)/2)`) produces the identical list,
confirming `2·A k + k = k² + 2`.

The values `1, 1, 2, 4, 7, 11, 16, 22, 29, 37, 46, 56, …` are the shifted
**central polygonal numbers** / "lazy caterer" sequence **OEIS A000124**
(`a(n) = n(n+1)/2 + 1`), read from `n = -1`. In particular `A k = A000124(k-1)` for

tends to `1` (it does not oscillate), and it therefore avoids the golden ratio that
governs the Fibonacci sequence.

## 1. A universal error law for greedy sum-avoiding sequences

**Conjecture.** For each fixed window width `w`, the greedy sequence that forbids every
new term from equalling the sum of its `w` predecessors grows as `A(n) = c_w n² + O(n)`
with an explicit rational `c_w`, and the rounded residual is eventually periodic.

*The key insight is* that greedy avoidance with a bounded window makes the sequence of
first differences a finite-state process, so the differences are ultimately arithmetic
and can be summed in closed form, pinning the quadratic constant exactly.

**Why now?** The two-back case has just been resolved with an exact closed form and a
provable growth constant of `1/2`; the same difference-telescoping method transfers
verbatim to wider windows, turning a family of folklore experiments into theorems.

## 2. Additive rigidity of quadratic avoidance sets

**Conjecture.** The value set `{1 + k(k-1)/2}` is additively rigid: its representation
function (the number of ways to write `n` as a sum of two members) is bounded, and it
contains no nontrivial additive quadruples.

*The key insight is* that the closed form turns every additive coincidence into a Pell-
type quadratic Diophantine equation, whose solution count is controlled by the classical
theory of binary quadratic forms.

**Why now?** With the exact formula in hand, additive questions that were previously
opaque become concrete Diophantine problems with mature tools available to attack them.

## 3. The ratio limit as a dividing line between growth regimes

**Conjecture.** A sequence has consecutive ratio tending to `1` exactly when it has
polynomial growth, while a homogeneous linear recurrence with dominant root `r > 1`
always has consecutive ratio tending to `r`. The value `1` cleanly separates polynomial
sequences from genuinely exponential ones.

*The key insight is* that the golden ratio is not special to Fibonacci but is simply its
dominant characteristic root, and the anti-Fibonacci limit `1` is the universal signature
of polynomial growth — so the ratio limit itself is a classifier.

**Why now?** The side-by-side contrast — golden ratio for Fibonacci, `1` for anti-
Fibonacci — supplies both endpoints of the dichotomy and makes the general statement the
obvious next target.

## 4. A genuinely oscillating anti-Fibonacci

**Conjecture.** There is a naturally defined greedy variant whose consecutive ratio has
limit inferior `1` and limit superior `2` and never converges, with the ratios
equidistributing over `[1, 2]` against an explicit measure.

*The key insight is* that oscillation between `1` and `2` — the behaviour the original
brief mistakenly attributed to the quadratic sequence — can be engineered by a rule that
alternately forbids the sum and forces near-doubling, realizing the intended phenomenon

**Why now?** Having shown the plain quadratic sequence does *not* oscillate, the natural
scientific move is to isolate exactly which avoidance rule does, closing the loop on the
brief's original intuition.

import Novelty.FangMultiset

/-!
# Congruence Consequences of the Digit-Multiset Framework

This file derives the classical mod-9 and mod-3 congruences of vampire
factorisations *as consequences* of the multiset additivity law
`FangMultiset.fangPair_digitsum` proved in `Novelty.FangMultiset`, together with
the standard "casting out nines" fact `n ≡ digitsum n [MOD 9]`.

The dependency direction is one-way:

  digit multiset  ──►  `fangPair_digitsum` (multiset arithmetic only)
                  ──►  mod-9 / mod-3 congruences (this file).

No congruence is used in the proof of the additivity law, so the derivation is
free of circular reasoning.

## Main results

* `cast_out_nine` — the base-10 casting-out-nines fact restated for `digitsum`,
  a thin wrapper over the catalog/Mathlib lemma `Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum`.
* `fangPair_modEq_nine` / `fangPair_prod_modEq_nine` — the vampire law
  `v ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`, i.e. `x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`.
* `fangPair_modEq_three` — the mod-3 shadow `v ≡ x + y [MOD 3]`.
* `fang_not_one_mod_three` — the arithmetic taboo: no fang is `≡ 1 (mod 3)`.

These reproduce, in the multiset framework, the invariants proved in the
catalog's `FINAL/` bestiary
(`Applications/NumericalMonsters.sharesAllDigits_modEq_nine` and
`fang_not_one_mod_three`); here they are obtained strictly downstream of the
digit-sum additivity law rather than in tandem with it.
-/

namespace FangMultiset

/-- **Casting out nines.**  Every natural number is congruent to its base-10
digit sum modulo `9`.  A restatement of `Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum` in terms of
`digitsum`. -/
theorem cast_out_nine (n : ℕ) : n ≡ digitsum n [MOD 9] := by
  simpa [digitsum] using Nat.modEq_nine_digits_sum n

/-- **The vampire law modulo 9.**  A fang pair satisfies `v ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`.
The proof chains casting-out-nines with the *additivity of the digit sum*
(`fangPair_digitsum`); no congruence enters the additivity step. -/
theorem fangPair_modEq_nine (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    v ≡ x + y [MOD 9] := by
  have hd := fangPair_digitsum v x y h
  calc v ≡ digitsum v [MOD 9] := cast_out_nine v
    _ = digitsum x + digitsum y := hd.symm
    _ ≡ x + y [MOD 9] := ((cast_out_nine x).add (cast_out_nine y)).symm

/-- The product form of the vampire law: `x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9]`. -/
theorem fangPair_prod_modEq_nine (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 9] := by
  have h9 := fangPair_modEq_nine v x y h
  rw [h.2]; exact h9

/-- **The vampire law modulo 3.**  The mod-9 law casts down to `v ≡ x + y [MOD 3]`
since `3 ∣ 9`. -/
theorem fangPair_modEq_three (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    v ≡ x + y [MOD 3] :=
  (fangPair_modEq_nine v x y h).of_dvd (by norm_num)

/-- **Arithmetic taboo.**  For a fang pair, neither fang is congruent to `1`
modulo `3`.  Verified against `1260 = 21 · 60`: `21 % 3 = 0` and `60 % 3 = 0`. -/
theorem fang_not_one_mod_three (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    x % 3 ≠ 1 ∧ y % 3 ≠ 1 := by
  have h3 : x * y ≡ x + y [MOD 3] :=
    (fangPair_prod_modEq_nine v x y h).of_dvd (by norm_num)
  constructor
  · intro hx1
    have hxmod : x ≡ 1 [MOD 3] := by unfold Nat.ModEq; simpa using hx1
    have hchain : (1 * y) ≡ (1 + y) [MOD 3] :=
      ((hxmod.mul_right y).symm.trans h3).trans (hxmod.add_right y)
    have : (1 * y) % 3 = (1 + y) % 3 := hchain
    omega
  · intro hy1
    have hymod : y ≡ 1 [MOD 3] := by unfold Nat.ModEq; simpa using hy1
    have hchain : (x * 1) ≡ (x + 1) [MOD 3] :=
      ((hymod.mul_left x).symm.trans h3).trans (hymod.add_left x)
    have : (x * 1) % 3 = (x + 1) % 3 := hchain
    omega

/-! ### Non-vacuity witnesses -/

/-- On the smallest vampire: `1260 ≡ 21 + 60 [MOD 9]` (i.e. `0 ≡ 0`). -/
example : (1260 : ℕ) ≡ 21 + 60 [MOD 9] :=
  fangPair_modEq_nine 1260 21 60 ⟨by decide, by norm_num⟩

/-- Consistency with the taboo: neither `21` nor `60` is `≡ 1 (mod 3)`. -/
example : (21 : ℕ) % 3 ≠ 1 ∧ (60 : ℕ) % 3 ≠ 1 :=
  fang_not_one_mod_three 1260 21 60 ⟨by decide, by norm_num⟩

end FangMultiset

import Mathlib

/-!
# The Digit-Multiset Framework for Vampire Numbers (foundations)

This file develops the *digit-multiset* foundations of the vampire-number theory
from first principles about base-10 digit representation and multiset arithmetic.
It is deliberately kept free of any congruence reasoning: the mod-9 / mod-3
consequences are derived *afterwards* in `Novelty.FangCongruence`, so that there
is no circular dependency (the congruences are consequences of the additivity
laws proved here, not the other way around).

## Design: avoiding circular reasoning

The one primitive object is `multiset_of_digits n`, the multiset of base-10
digits of `n`.  Two structural invariants are read off it:

* `digitsum n = (multiset_of_digits n).sum`  (Lemma 1), and
* `len n = (multiset_of_digits n).card`       (Lemma 2).

The *fang* relation `IsFangPair v x y` says that the digit multiset of `v` is the
(multiset) sum of the digit multisets of the two fangs `x` and `y`, together with
`x * y = v`.  Because `Multiset.sum` and `Multiset.card` are additive over
`Multiset.+`, the two structural additivity laws

* `digitsum x + digitsum y = digitsum v`  (`fangPair_digitsum`), and
* `len v = len x + len y`                  (`fangPair_len`)

follow *purely* from multiset algebra — **no** casting-out-nines, **no** modular
arithmetic is used here.

## Relation to the catalog's verified results

The catalog's `FINAL/` bestiary (`Applications/NumericalMonsters/…`) states the
fang relation as a *list permutation* `SharesAllDigits b x y`.  Multiset equality
`(l₁ : Multiset _) = (l₂ : Multiset _)` is definitionally the same information as
`l₁.Perm l₂` (`Multiset.coe_eq_coe`), and `Multiset.sum`/`Multiset.card` on a
coerced list agree with `List.sum`/`List.length`
(`Multiset.sum_coe`, `Multiset.coe_card`).  So the additivity laws below are the
multiset-native restatement of the permutation facts `List.Perm.sum_eq` /
`List.Perm.length_eq` used there, packaged so the mod-9 law becomes a clean
downstream corollary.
-/

namespace FangMultiset

/-- The multiset of base-10 digits of `n` (the coercion of the digit *list*
`Nat.digits 10 n` to a `Multiset`).  This forgets the ordering of the digits
while keeping their multiplicities, which is exactly the data a vampire
factorisation must preserve. -/
def multiset_of_digits (n : ℕ) : Multiset ℕ := (Nat.digits 10 n : Multiset ℕ)

/-- The base-10 digit sum of `n`. -/
def digitsum (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (Nat.digits 10 n).sum

/-- The number of base-10 digits of `n`. -/
def len (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (Nat.digits 10 n).length

/-- **Lemma 1.**  The digit sum is the sum of the digit multiset.  This is a
basic property of digit representation: `Multiset.sum` on a coerced list is the
`List.sum` of that list. -/
theorem digitsum_eq_multiset_sum (n : ℕ) :
    digitsum n = (multiset_of_digits n).sum := by
  simp [digitsum, multiset_of_digits]

/-- **Lemma 2.**  The digit length is the cardinality of the digit multiset.
`Multiset.card` on a coerced list is the `List.length` of that list. -/
theorem len_eq_multiset_card (n : ℕ) :
    len n = (multiset_of_digits n).card := by
  simp [len, multiset_of_digits]

/-- **The fang-pair relation.**  `v` is a fang pair of `x` and `y` when the digit
multiset of `v` is the multiset sum of the digit multisets of `x` and `y`, and
`x * y = v`.  Multiset equality encodes precisely that the digits of `v` are a
permutation of the digits of `x` together with the digits of `y`. -/
def IsFangPair (v x y : ℕ) : Prop :=
  multiset_of_digits v = multiset_of_digits x + multiset_of_digits y ∧ x * y = v

/-- **Additivity of the digit sum.**  From a fang pair, the digit sums add:
`digitsum x + digitsum y = digitsum v`.  The proof is pure multiset arithmetic —
`Multiset.sum` is a homomorphism for `Multiset.+` (`Multiset.sum_add`) — and uses
no congruence property whatsoever. -/
theorem fangPair_digitsum (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    digitsum x + digitsum y = digitsum v := by
  obtain ⟨hm, _⟩ := h
  rw [digitsum_eq_multiset_sum, digitsum_eq_multiset_sum, digitsum_eq_multiset_sum,
    hm, Multiset.sum_add]

/-- **Additivity of the digit length.**  From a fang pair, the digit lengths add:
`len v = len x + len y`.  The proof is pure multiset arithmetic — `Multiset.card`
is a homomorphism for `Multiset.+` (`Multiset.card_add`) — and uses no congruence
property whatsoever. -/
theorem fangPair_len (v x y : ℕ) (h : IsFangPair v x y) :
    len v = len x + len y := by
  obtain ⟨hm, _⟩ := h
  rw [len_eq_multiset_card, len_eq_multiset_card, len_eq_multiset_card,
    hm, Multiset.card_add]

/-! ### Non-vacuity witness -/

/-- The smallest vampire number `1260 = 21 · 60` is a fang pair: the digit
multiset `{0,6,2,1}` of `1260` is the multiset sum of `{1,2}` and `{0,6}`. -/
example : IsFangPair 1260 21 60 := ⟨by decide, by norm_num⟩

/-- On the smallest vampire: `digitsum 21 + digitsum 60 = digitsum 1260` (namely
`3 + 6 = 9`). -/
example : digitsum 21 + digitsum 60 = digitsum 1260 :=
  fangPair_digitsum 1260 21 60 ⟨by decide, by norm_num⟩

/-- On the smallest vampire: `len 1260 = len 21 + len 60` (namely `4 = 2 + 2`). -/
example : len 1260 = len 21 + len 60 :=
  fangPair_len 1260 21 60 ⟨by decide, by norm_num⟩

end FangMultiset

All checks below were run with Lean `#eval` over `Nat.digits 10` and small brute force.

- `digits 10 1260 = [0, 6, 2, 1]`
- `digits 10 21 ++ digits 10 60 = [1, 2, 0, 6]`  → same multiset `{0,1,2,6}` as `1260`.

So `1260 = 21 · 60` is a fang pair, both fangs have two digits, and not both are
divisible by ten: **`1260` is a genuine vampire number.**

The first vampire numbers (OEIS **A014575**): 1260, 1395, 1435, 1530, 1827, 2187,
6880, 102510, 104260, 105210, ... with fang factorizations

| v    | fangs   |
|------|---------|
| 1260 | 21 · 60 |
| 1395 | 15 · 93 |
| 1435 | 35 · 41 |
| 1530 | 30 · 51 |
| 1827 | 21 · 87 |
| 2187 | 27 · 81 |
| 6880 | 80 · 86 |

For each pair above `x·y mod 9 = x+y mod 9`:

| v    | x  | y  | xy%9 | (x+y)%9 |
|------|----|----|------|---------|
| 1260 | 21 | 60 | 0    | 0       |
| 1395 | 15 | 93 | 0    | 0       |

| 1530 | 30 | 51 | 0    | 0       |
| 1827 | 21 | 87 | 0    | 0       |

| v    | x%3 | y%3 |
|------|-----|-----|
| 1260 | 0   | 0   |
| 1395 | 0   | 0   |
| 1435 | 2   | 2   |

| 1827 | 0   | 0   |
| 2187 | 0   | 0   |

`125460 = 204 · 615 = 246 · 510` is the "zombie"-flavoured example from the brief:

# Future Directions — Vampire Numbers and the Fang Congruence

## 1. The mod-9 residue distribution is asymptotically saturated
Every digit-preserving factorization forces `(x-1)(y-1) ≡ 1` modulo nine, so the
residue pair of the two factors is trapped in a small, explicit solution set. The
bold conjecture is that this trap is not merely a constraint but is filled to
capacity: over all vampire numbers up to a growing bound, the pair of factor
residues equidistributes across exactly the admissible classes and never strays
outside them. **The key insight is** that the mod-nine obstruction born from digit
sums behaves like a random variable that hits every allowed value with its fair
share of the mass. **Why now?** The obstruction itself is settled, so what remains
is a self-contained equidistribution question, decoupled entirely from the
difficulty of factoring.

## 2. A stacked modular sieve that removes a positive fraction — but never all
The mod-9 law and its mod-3 corollary already reject most candidates without any
factoring. Layering independent digit-sum-driven congruences across several moduli
yields a single cheap sieve every vampire must survive. The conjecture is that the
survivors that are nonetheless not vampires retain a density strictly between zero
and one: the sieve is powerful yet provably incomplete. **The key insight is** that
digit-multiset preservation contributes one genuinely new congruence per compatible
modulus, and these constraints do not collapse into one another. **Why now?** Each
constituent congruence is individually proved, so the frontier is simply measuring
how much the combined test can and cannot decide.

## 3. Ghost numbers vanish geometrically in digit length
A ghost number multiplies two nontrivial factors while sharing no digit with either
of them. As the digit length grows, demanding that a product dodge every digit of
both factors becomes an increasingly improbable coincidence. The conjecture is a
geometric decay: the ghost count below a `d`-digit ceiling is dominated by a term
shrinking like a fixed fraction raised to the power `d`. **The key insight is** that
digit avoidance is a large-deviation event, and a clean union bound over the digit
classes captures its exponential rarity. **Why now?** The definition is elementary
and the governing heuristic is a textbook probabilistic bound, so a rigorous ceiling
on ghost density needs no heavy machinery.

## 4. Vampires are guaranteed in every even-length block by design
Numerics suggest each even-length decimal block contains a vampire, yet existence is
usually stumbled upon rather than engineered. The conjecture is that a constructive
family of factor pairs — each built from a digit-balanced core plus a controlled
tail — can be shown to multiply into the intended block while permuting, never
losing, their digits, proving vampires occur in every even-length block and hence
with bounded gaps in digit length. **The key insight is** that multiplying two
digit-controlled, near-palindromic factors can force the product to rearrange rather
than destroy digits, turning digit preservation into a design property. **Why now?**
The smallest vampire is verified and the exact digit-sum and digit-count identities
any such construction must obey are already in hand, giving precise blueprints.

## 5. The whole bestiary is a shadow of the `(b-1)` law
In base `b` the digit sum is congruent to the number itself modulo `b-1`, so the
entire fang phenomenon should reappear with `9` replaced by `b-1`. The conjecture is
that in every base any digit-preserving factorization satisfies `x·y ≡ x+y` modulo
`b-1`, and the primes dividing `b-1` generate factor obstructions generalizing the
base-ten mod-3 rule — so bases whose predecessor is highly composite make vampires
rarest. **The key insight is** that the complete theory is governed by a single
identity, `digit sum ≡ value mod (b-1)`, handing control of the bestiary to the
arithmetic of `b-1`. **Why now?** The base-ten case is fully established, so the leap
is a reparameterization that immediately predicts a base-dependent hierarchy of
vampire scarcity ready for testing.

concept.title: Phantom Topologies: Spaces That Change When You Look at Them
concept.concept_description: What if the topology of a space depended on who is observing it? Define a phantom topology on a set X as a function T: O -> Top(X) that assigns to each observer o a topology T(o) on X. Two observers o1, o2 agree on an open set U if U is open in both T(o1) and T(o2). The phantom number of (X, T) is the minimum number of observers needed to determine the topology: if U is open in every T(o) that contains a point x, then U is a neighborhood of x in the 'real' topology. Conjecture: Every second-countable space (X, tau) admits a phantom representation with at most 2 observers (the real topology is the intersection of two phantom topologies).
